233.t: Quitting school at 14 to sell ice and coal for Mr. Cooper
233.s: In Depression Columbus, Monk quit school and worked at a coal and ice shed, learning to drive in a Model A truck for $6 a week.
233.q: Right, hard times, yeah. I remember the Depression very, very clearly. I quit school and went to work, and I was working in an ice and coal yard.

233.t: His father's wholesale fruit and vegetable job
233.s: His father earned $15 a week unloading boxcars of produce, and Monk worked alongside him.
233.q: He was working for the owners of this company, wholesale fruits and vegetables, so he was a truck driver. His job was more or less like he would unload the boxcars that would come in, from wherever they shipped stuff in from. Where the fruits and vegetables come in, he'd unload them from the…

233.t: Back to Indianapolis at 19: foundry job, first car, mother's home
233.s: Monk and Wes returned to their mother and stepfather; he took a foundry job at $21 a week and bought a car.
233.q: : It was late for me, it was very late. Because when I left Columbus at the age of 19, and when I moved to Indianapolis -- Wes and I moved there together because my older brother had passed on -- Wes and I came back to Indianapolis. And I went to work in the foundries when I got there. My folks…

627.t: Williams's hard childhood, welfare and raising his siblings
627.s: Williams describes walking with his mother to the welfare office, a $12 monthly job, sleeping in barns, and raising his siblings without a father.
627.ch: Williams on hard times and money
627.q: But that's all it paid. But, I remember so that we couldn't get no work. And me and my mother would walk from Baker every day trying to get on the welfare to get help. That's right. The other way, you see, I raised up my sisters and brothers without a father. I haven't had it rough all my days. I…

668.t: Depression-era childhood and nine foster homes
668.s: Davern recalls little music at home beyond bouncing to the radio, and reveals he was in nine foster homes before age six.

491.t: Welfare, hand-me-down clothes and moving to Page Street
491.s: His father had left; the family was on welfare, ate government food, then improved with the WPA era, took in roomers on Page Street and got the saxophone.
491.q: Elementary school. When I went to school, we always knew who was on welfare, because they gave us clothes too. The clothes – the pants that they gave us, for the kids, they always reminded me of pallbearers pants, with the stripes and everything. It looked like everybody was going to a funeral,…

471.t: Mother's work, sister Eleanor and boyhood hustles
471.s: His parents separated when he was seven; his mother did domestic work, he minded his sister and earned money shining shoes, delivering papers and hauling ice, and a neighbor bought him records.
471.ch: Growing up and learning drums in Washington
471.q: By the time I got to be seven years old, I was separated – my mother and father were separated. So my mother pulled the duty of taking care of me and my sister by herself. She was a domestic worker. She used to work in people’s houses later for $15, $20 an hour, to take care of us all her life.…

231.s: He works in a packing house and gets a Billy goat his father harnesses to a wagon.
231.q: stamping meat. I worked there for, oh, maybe a year. Then I once saw a Billy goat and I wanted my father to get me a Billy goat, but he didn't want me to have a goat, he wanted me to have a pony. So while he was working for the Nashville Saddlery Company, he made a set of harness for a pony; but I…

385.t: Hometown, parents, and his birth date
385.s: He went back to Virginia once, knew his parents little, sold papers as a boy, and worked at a cleaning and pressing shop.
385.ch: Three Deuces and 52nd Street with Tatum
385.q: No I didn't know them that well. She stayed in the Church a lot, and I was out in the street. Shiniw shoes -- I'd be gettin' up 5 o'clock in the mornin' sellin' newspapers -- The Times-Herald. I did the regular hustle that the fellows do. There was no robbin' and stealin' like they do now...

86.t: Farm work and the coal-mining uncle
86.s: Edison describes the hard farm chores, what they grew, and his uncle's miner wages.
86.q: Physical, oh, gee whiz. You know, it's like the -- it was an old comedy team years ago, comedian named John Mason. He was a funny man. He said he never did like the farm because there were too many "ups" on it. You get up every morning -- he wasn't kidding. It was a hard job. But I had to hoe the…

455.t: Learning to drive and summer work at the Studebaker plant
455.s: His father kept his job through the Depression; Budd learned to drive delivering cars and earned good money unloading freight cars.
455.q: He got so good till when the Depression hit they couldn't fire him. They didn't fire him. They didn't want to fire him, because he was like doing the job of three men, I guess, to keep his job, there handling all those departments in there, and this is one of the places I learned to drive, because…
